title: Anterior part of fronto-temporal language network as the neural basis of morphologically structured word form processing: evidence from Korean morphologically complex word.
abstract: The present fMRI study investigated which subregions of the visual word recognition network contribute to morphologically structured word form processing in Korean. Participants performed two separate lexical decision tasks in the scanner. In the Eojeol task, stimuli were three-syllable words composed of a disyllabic noun plus a case particle, whereas in the Noun task, stimuli were disyllabic (DSN) and trisyllabic (TSN) nouns. Behaviorally, reaction time was significantly longer in the Eojeol condition than in both DSN and TSN conditions, indicating greater processing demands for morphologically complex words, while accuracy did not differ across conditions. At the neural level, ROI analyses revealed that Eojeol processing elicited stronger activation than simple nouns in specific nodes of the visual word recognition related system, including the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis), anterior perisylvian cortex, anterior superior temporal sulcus, and anterior inferior temporal gyrus. These findings suggest that morphologically complex word recognition in Korean recruits additional resources within the visual word recognition network, highlighting the role of anterior fronto-temporal subregions in combining content and functional morphemes into unified lexical representations.

title: A latent genetic factor underlies multiple component phenotypes of cerebral small vessel disease.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) encompasses white matter hyperintensities (WMH), enlarged perivascular spaces (PVS), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), small vessel stroke (SVS), and cognitive impairment-phenotypes that frequently co-occur yet have been studied as independent genetic endpoints. Whether a shared genetic architecture underlies these co-occurring cSVD-related phenotypes remains unclear. We applied Genomic SEM to GWAS summary statistics from six phenotypes (WMH, PVS, ICH, SVS, cognitive performance, systolic blood pressure), followed by multivariate association scanning, Bayesian fine-mapping (SuSiE/FINEMAP), gene-level (MAGMA) and transcriptome-wide (sCCA-TWAS/FOCUS) analyses, pathway enrichment, cell-type specificity (CELLECT) and spatial developmental mapping (gsMap). A common-factor model fit the data well (CFI = 1.00, SRMR = 0.061). The multivariate scan identified 1,423 genome-wide significant SNPs, resolving into 20 independent lead SNPs mapped to 14 distinct genomic loci, of which 2 were not detected at genome-wide significance in any constituent single-trait GWAS. Fine-mapping prioritized three high-confidence causal variants at EFEMP1, ICOSLG, and AC098824.6. Gene-level and transcriptome-wide analyses converged on effector genes at 17q25.1 (TRIM47/TRIM65), 10q24.33 (SH3PXD2A), and 2q33.1 (NBEAL1). MAGMA additionally identified APOE at 19q13.32. Pathway analysis highlighted epigenetic dysregulation, cellular senescence, and amyloid fiber formation. CELLECT identified vascular endothelial cells and pericytes as enriched cell types. gsMap revealed developmental enrichment in lung, kidney, and meninges exceeding brain tissue. These findings delineate a coherent latent genetic structure linking multiple cSVD-related phenotypes, rooted in vascular wall cell biology, epigenetic regulation, and cellular senescence, with developmental origins spanning multiple organ microvascular beds.

title: Stable Isotope Labeling by Amino Acids in Cell Culture (SILAC) for Quantitative Proteomics.
journal: Advances in experimental medicine and biology
abstract: Stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) is a powerful approach for high-throughput quantitative proteomics. SILAC allows highly accurate protein quantitation through metabolic encoding of whole cell proteomes using stable isotope-labeled amino acids. Since its introduction in 2002, SILAC has become increasingly popular. In this chapter, we review the methodology and application of SILAC, with an emphasis on three research areas: dynamics of posttranslational modifications, protein-protein interactions, and protein turnover.

title: Stress-induced reinstatement of nicotine conditioned place preference in a rodent model of dopamine dysregulation: genetic, behavioral and molecular correlates of drug abuse vulnerability.
abstract: Schizophrenia and related psychoses are accompanied by poor stress adaptation and a high prevalence of cigarette smoking, contributing to reduced treatment adherence and poor quality of life. The mechanistic contributions to stress-induced drug-seeking in psychosis remain poorly understood. The present study evaluated nicotine conditioned place preference (CPP) stress reinstatement in a heritable rodent model of dopamine dysregulation relevant to psychosis, alongside molecular and epigenetic alterations associated with drug use vulnerability. Adolescent offspring (F1) of Sprague-Dawley rats treated neonatally with saline (MSxFS) or quinpirole (MQxFQ) were assessed for nicotine CPP expression, extinction, and restraint stress-induced reinstatement. One hour following stress, nucleus accumbens (NAc) and amygdala tissue were analyzed for CREB and dynorphin expression, with complementary single-nucleus RNA sequencing used to identify cell-type-specific genetic adaptations in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of adolescent rats. MQxFQ rats exhibited enhanced nicotine CPP, resistance to extinction, and robust stress-induced reinstatement relative to MSxFS controls. Following nicotine and stress exposure, MQxFQ rats showed reduced CREB in the NAc and increased CREB and dynorphin in the amygdala. Differential gene expression profiling in the mPFC revealed cell-type specific metabolic and plasticity-related neuroadaptations consistent with cortical vulnerability to psychosis and drug use. These findings demonstrate significant expression of stress-induced reinstatement in a heritable model of dopamine dysregulation. Convergent molecular and genetic adaptations implicate dysregulated stress and reward circuitry, providing a mechanistic framework linking genetic risk for psychosis to maladaptive drug-seeking and vulnerability to stress.

title: Lipid-fuelled synaptic plasticity: integrating membrane turnover, β-oxidation, and protein lipidation.
abstract: Synaptic plasticity requires the coordinated regulation of membrane remodelling, energy production, and protein turnover. However, how these processes are integrated at the molecular level remains unclear. Here, we propose that activity-dependent lipid flux represents a central mechanism linking these processes. Saturated free fatty acids (sFFAs) released from membrane phospholipids, triglycerides, or from extracellular uptake can be activated to acyl-CoA and directed to mitochondrial β-oxidation and synaptic protein lipidation. These represent two emerging pathways adding to the complexity of roles played by sFFAs, including membrane fluidity and receptor activation. Recent work identifies DDHD2 as a mechanistic entry point into this broader synaptic lipid network. We position DDHD2-dependent lipid mobilisation in the wider context of glia-neuron lipid transfer and ApoE/sortilin-dependent fatty acid uptake. Key unresolved questions include the source and fate of fatty acids, the relative contribution of β-oxidation versus glycolysis to ATP production, and whether these pathways are altered in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Modeling and parameter estimation of tumor spheroids from bottom-view imaging: beyond the spherical assumption.
abstract: Tumor spheroids are widely used in vitro models for studying tumor growth and treatment response, yet their analysis is often limited by incomplete geometric measurements. In practice, only a two-dimensional bottom view is available, which can lead to strong biases when spheroids deviate from an ideal spherical shape, in particular for flattened aggregates. We propose a mechanistic modeling and data assimilation framework that accounts for both poor data quality and model uncertainty. A biologically motivated partial differential equations model with axial symmetry is introduced and reduced to a low-dimensional system compatible with sparse observations and ellipsoidal shapes. Uncertainties in initial conditions and parameters are handled using a Luenberger-type observer coupled with a reduced-order unscented Kalman filter. The approach is validated on synthetic data and applied to experimental in vitro spheroid data under propranolol treatment, illustrating how model-based integration of limited measurements improves the interpretation of spheroid growth dynamics and treatment-induced morphological changes.

title: Architecture of the Norrin signaling complex and structure-guided surrogate design.
abstract: Norrin binds Frizzled 4 (FZD4), tetraspanin 12 (TSPAN12) and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) to regulate angiogenesis and the integrity of the blood-brain barrier and inner blood-retina barrier (BRB). Aberrant Norrin signal causes retinopathies, BRB defects and deafness. Therapeutic mimetics of Norrin are currently in clinical trials for eye diseases. To characterize the mechanism of Norrin signal biogenesis, we determined the structure of a Norrin-FZD4-TSPAN12-LRP5 signaling complex using a de novo designed FZD4 binder as a 'protein glue'. Our structure shows that two curved Norrin homodimers bridge two FZD4-TSPAN12 heterodimers. LRP5LA3 simultaneously interacts with TSPAN12 and two Norrin homodimers, positioning the cytosolic FZD4 and LRP5 tails for signal activation. On the basis of our findings, we designed FZD4CRD-LRP5LA3 bispecific binders that act as Norrin surrogates. Our signaling assays showed that oligomerization of the Norrin surrogate enhances signaling potency. Thus, this work reveals how the Norrin signal is generated and may assist in the development of Norrin/Wnt mimetics.

title: Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 rescues adult hippocampal neurogenesis and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease via regulating BDNF/TrkB signaling.
abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) occurs throughout lifespan of humans and rodents and is correlated with memory performance and cognitive plasticity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), AHN is impeded, while the molecular basis behind this impairment remains to be elucidated. Here we identified Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 (BCAS2), a core component of the CDC5L/Prp19 spliceosome complex, regulating AHN in AD. Using Bcas2 conditional knockout mice, AD mouse model APP/PS1 mice, established mouse primary adult neural stem cells and single cell sequencing, we demonstrate that BCAS2 replacement in adult mouse hippocampus promotes NSC activation and differentiation to neuron, restore AHN and relevant memory deficits through BDNF/TrkB signaling. Our findings corroborate the significance of AHN in AD and reveal the possible therapeutic potential of targeting BCAS2 in neurodegeneration.

title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes.
abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits.
abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51- astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

title: Functional architecture of the human insula.
abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1.
abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine-threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. 'Sleepy', a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries.
abstract: Maternal caregiving requires sensory vigilance to ensure offspring survival, particularly during sleep. Infant cries are salient sensory cues that reliably trigger maternal arousal and caregiving responses in both humans and dams, but the underlying neural circuitry remains poorly defined. Here we identify a corticohypothalamic circuit in mice that mediates maternal awakening in response to pup calls. We show that layer 6 (L6) neurons in the temporal association cortex and ectorhinal cortex (TeA/Ect) projecting to the preoptic area (POA) exhibit enhanced responsiveness to pup calls after the transition to motherhood. This enhanced responsiveness is mediated by increased expression of dopamine receptor D1 (Drd1) in TeA/Ect → POA neurons. Additionally, we reveal a pathway from the auditory thalamus to L6 TeA/Ect neurons that transmits pup cues during sleep. Together, these findings identify a dedicated neural circuit that grants infant cries privileged access to arousal systems, likely representing a fundamental adaptation for caregiving across mammals.

title: Evolution towards higher unitary conductance in mammals makes BK channels more efficient and precise.
abstract: The large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BK) channel plays a critical role in neuronal excitability and spike timing precision. Mammalian BK channels are distinguished by an exceptionally high unitary conductance (~250 pS), while invertebrates exhibit a significantly lower unitary conductance. We confirmed the evolutionary trend to high unitary conductance and used computational models to examine how differences in unitary conductance affect calcium activation of BK channels and influence neuronal dynamics. We show that mammalian BK channels are activated more efficiently by calcium and generate stronger repolarizing currents than lower unitary conductance channels. Channels with lower unitary conductance require greater channel density in the cell membrane, leading to stronger competition for calcium and reduced activation. In contrast, high unitary conductance channels minimize competition, enabling more effective activation and repolarization. Incorporating these channel properties into a neuronal model revealed that mammalian-type BK channels enhance spike-timing precision, consistent with the evolution of fine motor control and advanced neuronal processing in mammals.

title: Oropouche virus disrupts neurodevelopment and exhibits congenital infection potential.
abstract: Oropouche virus (OROV) historically caused a self-limiting disease, yet recent strains have been clinically linked to congenital infection and neurodevelopmental disease. These observations highlight the need to study OROV as a congenital pathogen. Here, using both a historical and currently circulating strain, we show OROV infects neurons across differentiation states in human forebrain organoids. Compared with the neurotropic congenital pathogen Zika virus (ZIKV), OROV exhibits a heightened capacity for neuroinfection and pathology in both forebrain organoids and neonatal mice. The increased permissiveness of OROV is driven, in part, by a broader neuronal tropism and a relative insensitivity to neuronal type I interferon-mediated antiviral responses. Consistent with clinical observations, neonatal neuroinfection results in rapid and severe neuropathology marked by cerebral hemorrhage. Finally, using a transient type I interferon-blockade model, we demonstrate that OROV can productively infect the murine placenta and cause fetal growth restriction. Together, our complementary models support a unified framework in which placental and fetal barriers limit productive fetal brain infection, yet OROV exhibits marked neurotropism and neuropathogenic potential upon gaining access to developing neural tissues. These findings reinforce the need for vigilant monitoring of OROV as an emerging pathogen associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and congenital disease.

title: Coexistence of anhedonia and sensation-seeking with context-dependent gut dysbiosis in a prodromal transgenic mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Accumulating evidence indicates that gut microbiota plays a role in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Microbiota-based treatments for prodromal PD, which is accompanied by a wide range of neuropsychiatric symptoms, are being considered a potential early intervention but are still under-investigated. This study examined the association between symptoms of affective and motivational impairments and gut dysbiosis in a transgenic mouse model (line G2-3) that overexpresses A53T mutant α-synuclein, a key protein involved in the disease pathology. By introducing biologically meaningful variations, such as genotype-based social grouping, efforts have been made to strengthen validity of the results and their translational relevance. Behavioral assessment was conducted on 6-month-old mice (the premotor stage) using Open Field, Elevated Plus Maze, Sucrose Preference and Tail Suspension tests. Fecal microbiota of mice was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Obtained data revealed a strong behavioral phenotype in transgenic mice expressed as co-occurrence of consummatory anhedonia and sensation-seeking/risk-taking behavior, without significant motivational deficits and with variable gut dysbiosis: mixed-genotype housing, among others, prominently favored Bacteroidaceae/Bacteroides, as observed in PD patients, while single-genotype housing increased Dubosiella, a key bacteria in gut-originated PD model, along with the enrichment of Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, a well-known health-promoting bacterium. Overall, using a mouse model with adequate construct validity, this study identifies challenges in novel strategies that consider gut microbiota as an early diagnostic and therapeutic target for PD; it highlights the potential of the examined transgenic strain in studying low hedonic tone- and sensation-seeking-associated PD prodrome, building the basis for personalized medicine.

title: Autism with social anxiety is associated with acquiescent behaviors and enlarged amygdala volume.
abstract: Social anxiety (SA) frequently co-occurs with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but it remains unclear whether SA in ASD reflects greater symptom severity or a distinct subtype. Across two complementary studies, we characterized the behavioral and neural correlates of SA in ASD using a naturalistic social navigation task measuring affiliative and power-related behaviors. In Study 1 (ASD = 575; controls = 357), autistic individuals with SA exhibited significantly reduced task-derived power behaviors (e.g., compliance with others' requests) compared to those without SA-a pattern not observed in non-autistic individuals. In Study 2 (ASD = 72; controls = 72), individuals with both ASD and SA showed enlarged amygdala volumes relative to both ASD without SA and non-autistic individuals. These behavioral and neural differences found in Study 1 and Study 2 were not observed in ASD with co-occurring depression or generalized anxiety disorder. Moreover, in Study 2, larger amygdala volume in the ASD group was associated with reduced task-derived power behaviors, indicating a neural signature linking social-behavioral differences and anxiety-related features. Together, these findings point to a distinct ASD phenotype marked by social anxiety, altered interpersonal dynamics, and amygdala enlargement, with implications for diagnosis and tailored intervention.

title: Five-country analysis of geographic and dietary drivers of gut microbiome composition and genomic variation.
abstract: Human diet and lifestyle vary widely across cultures, shaping global diversity in gut microbiome composition and function. However, comparable cross-population studies have been limited by methodological heterogeneity. The Human Diets and Microbiome Initiative (THDMI) integrates standardized recruitment, dietary assessment, and shotgun metagenomics across 1,976 participants from the United States, United Kingdom, Spain, Mexico, and Japan to disentangle biological from technical variation. We observed pronounced geographic differences in nutrient intake, food consumption, and microbial composition, with both shared and country-specific features linked to diet. Sparse canonical correlation and machine-learning analyses revealed that microbiome-diet associations were largely population-specific, with limited cross-country generalization. Strain-level analyses further uncovered significant genomic differentiation of gut microbes, consistent with localized dietary and ecological differences. Together, these results show that while core microbial responses to healthy eating exist, the structure and function of the human gut microbiome varies strongly with culture, geography, and long-term dietary practices.

title: Structure and functional divergence of the non-canonical BoNT-like toxin PG1 and PG2.
abstract: Botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) are potent bacterial toxins. Distinct BoNT-like toxins, including BoNT/X, BoNT/En, and PMP1, form a distinct lineage. Here we characterize two additional members of this group, PG-toxin 1 and 2 (PG1 and PG2). Their light-chain (LC) and heavy-chain (HC) domains are encoded by adjacent genes. PG1 and PG2 LCs cleave Drosophila SNAP-25 at distinct sites (N196-E197 and R191-K193, respectively); PG1 is more potent, while PG2 activity depends on pH and ionic strength. Both LCs enter Sf9 cells via clathrin-mediated endocytosis. PG1 LC is toxic to Drosophila and northern armyworm independently of its HC, whereas PG2 LC toxicity is enhanced by its HC. Cryo-EM shows that PG1 adopts a distinct compact di-chain architecture with a door-hinge-like "belt." These findings expand the structural and functional diversity of the BoNT family and support the potential of PG-toxins as insecticidal agents and research tools.

title: Short-term memory of past caspase activity biases cell elimination in vivo.
abstract: Apoptosis is triggered by the activation of Caspases leading to irreversible engagement in cell death. However, recent data outline numerous non-apoptotic functions of caspases as well as quite ubiquitous sublethal activation of effector caspases in vivo, opening the question of what drives the bifurcation between cell death and survival. Using quantitative live imaging combined with machine learning and optogenetics in the Drosophila pupal notum (a single-layer epithelium), we reveal the existence of a large heterogeneity of caspase activity thresholds between cells and distinct spatial domains with low or high sensitivity to caspases. We outline the central role of past exposure to sublethal caspase activity, which sensitises cells to apoptosis for several hours and reduces their threshold, and can bias single-cell elimination. Altogether, this work reveals the role of a cell's past history for apoptosis regulation in vivo, which can bias clonal selection and the spatial pattern of cell death.

title: Multichannel, biomimetic scaffolds improve functional connectivity following traumatic long-gap peripheral nerve injury.
abstract: The gold standard for repair of peripheral nerve injuries is a nerve autograft. Donor nerve harvest creates a second surgical site, invariable numbness and donor site chronic neuropathic pain in 20% of cases. We developed a poly-caprolactone (PCL) multichannel, biomimetic scaffold with surface features promoting cell and vascular attachment and rapid, linear axonal regeneration. The cross-sectional area available for axonal regeneration exceeds that of autografts. When compared to nerve autografts and FDA-approved nerve conduits in 1cm-long rat and 3cm-long rabbit sciatic gap injury, biomimetic scaffolds were equivalent or superior to nerve autografts on measures of axonal regeneration, re-connection between gastrocnemius muscle and spinal cord motor neurons, and evoked motor responses. Scaffolds were superior in all measures to open tube conduits. Biomimetic multichannel scaffolds have potential to replace the need for autografting for peripheral nerve gap repair and are now undergoing multicenter clinical trials.

title: Rubicon modulates neuroimmune responses following traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) elicits robust neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, coupled with an acute inhibition of macro-autophagy (autophagy) in neurons and microglia. Rubicon (Rubcn), a Beclin1 interacting protein that suppresses autophagy and mediates LC3-associated phagocytosis and endocytosis (LAP/LANDO), influences inflammatory signaling in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammaging diseases; yet its role in acquired brain injury has not been examined. Using a controlled cortical impact model, we investigated the role of Rubicon in acute neuroinflammatory responses following injury by comparing wild-type and Rubcn-mutant mice. Bulk-RNA sequencing of injured cortex revealed attenuated induction of inflammatory pathways and reduced activation of pro-inflammatory microglial/macrophage phenotype in injured Rubcn-mutant mice. Rubcn-mutant mice demonstrated less pronounced inhibition of autophagy during the acute phase of injury. Although the inflammatory differences were transient, Rubicon mutant mice exhibited improved motor coordination and gait stability during recovery. Proteomic analyses revealed the presence of a truncated Rubicon protein in the mutant mice and identified the negative regulator of reactive oxygen species (NRROS) as a novel interactor of Rubicon. Consistent with this interaction, Rubcn-mutant mice displayed markedly reduced oxidative damage, indicated by decreased lipid peroxidation after injury. Together, these findings indicate that Rubicon promotes acute neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress responses following TBI by modulating autophagy and ROS production. Rubicon-mediated pathways may serve as therapeutic targets to attenuate inflammation-mediated damage after TBI.

title: Changes in Comorbid Obsessive-Compulsive and Restrictive Eating Disorder Symptoms in Eating Disorder Focused Family Therapy.
journal: The International journal of eating disorders
abstract: Restrictive eating disorders (EDs) are highly comorbid with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and comorbidity is associated with worsened outcomes. However, it is unclear if (1) Maudsley family therapy (FT-AN) for restrictive EDs reduces comorbid OCD symptoms, and (2) if higher baseline OCD symptoms merely reflect higher severity or are associated with inhibited ED treatment. Participants with restrictive EDs (Anorexia Nervosa, Atypical Anorexia Nervosa, or other specified feeding and eating disorders) received FT-AN as part of an intensive day program or outpatient services in London from mid-2024 through January 2026. Nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests examined pre/post differences in ED, OCD, and general impairment symptomology. Linear regressions investigated the effect of baseline OCD scores on changes in ED symptoms across treatment. Across FT-AN, ED pathology and weight improved while OCD pathology and general impairment did not. After excluding likely under-reporters, OCD symptoms and overall functioning did significantly improve. More severe OCD impairment at baseline did not impair, and in fact was related with more ED improvement. However, more severe ED and OCD symptoms at baseline were both associated with less change in weight. Together, these results suggest that worsened outcomes among patients with OCD represent higher initial severity rather than treatment inhibition. FT-AN's effects on ED symptoms are likely not directly inhibited by, but also do not appear to fully target, OCD symptoms. Future research should examine efficacy and optimal timing of incorporating OCD-specific treatments into care.

title: Structure-Activity Relationships of Glycine-Linked Kn2-7 Dimers and Polymyxin B-Related Peptides in the Enhancement of CpG DNA-Induced Macrophage Activation.
abstract: Kn2-7, an α-helical antimicrobial peptide, enhances the activation of mouse macrophage-like RAW264.7 cells in response to DNA containing unmethylated cytosine-guanine motifs (CpG DNA). We previously showed that high amphipathicity is an important determinant of the CpG DNA response-enhancing activity of short α-helical peptides. However, whether this principle applies to non-α-helical or larger amphipathic molecules is not clear. In the present study, polymyxin B (PMB), a non-α-helical amphipathic antimicrobial peptide, enhanced CpG DNA-induced activation of RAW264.7 cells, whereas PMB nonapeptide, which lacks the hydrophobic tail of PMB, did not. We also synthesized dimeric Kn2-7 peptides, Kn-Gly-Kn, Kn-(Gly)3-Kn, and Kn-(Gly)5-Kn, in which two Kn2-7 molecules are linked by one, three, or five glycine residues, respectively. Kn-(Gly)3-Kn and Kn-(Gly)5-Kn, but not Kn-Gly-Kn, retained CpG DNA response-enhancing activity. Peptide structure prediction using PEP-FOLD3 suggested that, in Kn-Gly-Kn, the hydrophobic faces of the two Kn2-7 domains are oriented toward each other, resulting in a less distinct overall amphipathic molecular organization. In contrast, the longer glycine linkers in Kn-(Gly)3-Kn and Kn-(Gly)5-Kn may increase conformational flexibility, allowing each α-helical Kn2-7 domain to function as an independent amphipathic unit. These findings suggest that amphipathic molecular organization is an important factor in enhancing CpG DNA-induced responses and that such enhancement can also occur with a non-α-helical peptide, as demonstrated for PMB.

title: Advances in neurological disease models and optimization of the laboratory animal environment for reproducible research.
abstract: Animal models of neurological diseases have evolved from phenotype-based systems to integrated platforms that link genetics, molecular signaling, synaptic physiology, neural circuits, behavior, and therapeutic responses. Simultaneously, increasingly precise phenotyping has revealed that experimental outcomes are strongly influenced by age, microbiological status, diet, housing, stress, previous experience, health status, and measurement methodology. This review considers these two developments to be complementary requirements for reliable experimental neuroscience. Studies on voltage-gated calcium channel mutants have shown that defined genetic alterations can produce age-dependent abnormalities in motor function, cognition, emotion, autonomic regulation, and seizure susceptibility. Studies on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-Calcium-calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling, epigenetic regulators, stress-related phenotypes, and fear memory circuits have further illustrated how animal models can be characterized across levels, from molecular mechanisms to neural ensembles and therapeutic rescues. Translation to common marmosets extends these approaches to primate sleep and epilepsy, while highlighting the effects of genetic diversity, spontaneous disease, handling, and colony management. In parallel, studies on germ-free animals, diet, the gut microbiota, barrier facilities, cage enrichment, telemetry, and veterinary monitoring have demonstrated that husbandry variables, rather than technical background, are biological determinants. Integrating rigorous disease model characterization with evidence-based husbandry, environmental control, and transparent reporting should improve the reproducibility and translational value of preclinical neuroscience research and the welfare of the animals used.

title: Incidence and predictors of urinary tract infections after sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor initiation in older adults hospitalized for heart failure.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are recommended for heart failure treatment across the spectrum of ejection fraction; however, by promoting glycosuria, they may increase the risk of urinary tract infection, particularly in older adults. To assess the 6-month incidence of urinary tract infection following sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor initiation in older patients hospitalized for heart failure, and to identify associated factors. This retrospective single-centre study included patients aged≥75 years hospitalized for heart failure in geriatric and cardiology wards, and initiated on a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor between January 2022 and December 2024. The primary outcome was physician-diagnosed antibiotic-treated suspected urinary tract infection within 6 months, investigated using multivariable logistic regression. Of 260 included patients, 147 were hospitalized in the cardiology ward and 113 in the geriatric ward. Physician-diagnosed antibiotic-treated suspected urinary tract infection was recorded in 45 patients, corresponding to 17.3% of the total cohort and 21.0% of patients with an ascertainable outcome; the upper bound under the extreme worst-case assumption was 35.0%. Incidence was higher in the geriatric ward than in the cardiology ward (26.6 vs. 10.2%). After age matching, female sex (odds ratio 3.15, 95% confidence interval 1.22-8.14), history of urinary tract infection (odds ratio 3.05, 95% confidence interval 1.25-7.42), diabetes mellitus (odds ratio 3.17, 95% confidence interval 1.32-7.60) and geriatric ward hospitalization (odds ratio 3.84, 95% confidence interval 1.62-9.07) were associated with increased odds of urinary tract infection, although only history of urinary tract infection remained robust across missing-outcome sensitivity analyses. Suspected urinary tract infection was frequent after sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor initiation in hospitalized older adults. History of urinary tract infection was the most robust predictor, supporting individualized risk assessment and monitoring rather than routine prophylaxis.

title: Microbial resistance from genotype to metabolic phenotype.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses an escalating global threat, yet surveillance and mechanistic understanding remain anchored in individual resistance genes, an approach that is inadequate for capturing the ecological, genomic, and metabolic complexity through which resistance emerges and spreads. In this opinion article, we argue that genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a principled framework for advancing AMR research beyond this gene-centric paradigm. Strain-resolved GEMs embed resistance determinants within metabolic networks, with the potential to generate quantitative, context-dependent phenotypic predictions, including minimum inhibitory concentrations and environment-conditional resistance, that sequence-based tools do not provide. Expanded GEM frameworks incorporating mobile genetic elements, horizontal gene transfer, and community-level interactions support ecology-aware resistance profiling. At the therapeutic level, whole-network modelling can identify metabolic vulnerabilities, synthetic lethal interactions, and microbiome-targeted strategies. Integrating GEMs with multiomics and data-driven approaches represents a critical step toward a mechanism-aware AMR platform connecting surveillance, diagnosis, and drug discovery.

title: [Digital phenotyping in psychiatry: Concepts, systems, and clinical implications].
abstract: Digital phenotyping uses smartphones, wearable devices, and embedded sensors to repeatedly quantify behavioral and physiological features in real-world settings. Its development in psychiatry raises conceptual, methodological, clinical, infrastructural, and ethical questions. This scoping review aimed to map the different understandings of digital phenotyping, their applications, and their main limitations. A scoping review was conducted. PubMed was searched for publications issued between January 1st, 2015, and December 31st, 2025. Publications directly addressing the conceptual foundations, methodologies, infrastructures, clinical applications, or ethical implications of digital phenotyping in psychiatry and mental health were eligible. The included publications were synthesized using thematic analysis. Forty-five publications were included and classified into five thematic domains: epistemology and epistemic injustice; clinical reasoning and decision models; sociotechnical systems and infrastructures; ethical considerations; and computational models and data-driven frameworks. Digital phenotyping enables the longitudinal assessment of mobility, sleep, activity, sociability, smartphone use, and selected physiological parameters. However, the resulting signals are shaped by device characteristics, sampling strategies, preprocessing decisions, and analytical models. Methodological heterogeneity, limited external validation, platform dependency, and unresolved issues concerning clinical integration and data governance currently restrict generalizability. Digital phenotyping may complement clinical interviews and improve the study of individual trajectories, but it does not provide an exhaustive representation of mental states or constitute a validated biomarker in itself. Its clinical value depends on methodological reproducibility, robust infrastructures, demonstrable decision-making utility, and contextual interpretation by clinicians.

title: [Therapeutic chatbots in psychiatry: Between relational simulation and the reshaping of care].
abstract: The rapid development of conversational agents, or chatbots, in mental health is part of a broader transformation of digital psychiatry. Alongside advances in artificial intelligence, digital phenotyping, and ecological momentary interventions, therapeutic chatbots challenge not only the practical organisation of care but also its epistemological and relational foundations. This article aims to critically examine their place in psychiatry, particularly with regard to therapeutic alliance, agency, and patient autonomy. We conducted a conceptual and narrative review of the literature on conversational agents in mental health. We examined the evolution and typology of chatbots, their clinical uses, available evidence regarding efficacy and acceptability, and the theoretical and ethical issues associated with their integration into psychiatric care. Particular attention was paid to the concepts of relational simulation, distributed agency, and attentional modulation. Available studies suggest that chatbots may produce modest short-term improvements in depressive and anxiety symptoms and may enhance engagement with digital interventions. However, their effects appear less consistent over the medium term, and concerns remain regarding data confidentiality, reliability, clinical integration, and human oversight. Evaluating chatbots solely according to their ability to reproduce a human therapeutic relationship may overlook their specific functions. Their clinical value may instead lie in their capacity to support self-monitoring, modulate attention, reinforce adaptive behaviours, and deliver contextualised interventions within a broader therapeutic system. Therapeutic chatbots should not be considered substitutes for clinicians, but rather hybrid components of distributed care systems combining human interaction, digital monitoring, and behavioural intervention. Their responsible integration requires robust clinical validation, transparent governance, respect for patient autonomy, and continued human supervision.

title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

title: Depression in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease: Clinical manifestations, biomarker evidence, and predictive implications.
abstract: Depression is one of the earliest and most frequent non-motor symptoms in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease (PD), often preceding motor signs by years to decades. This review synthesizes epidemiological, neuroimaging, biomarker, and genetic evidence to clarify whether depression is a risk factor, a direct prodromal manifestation, or both. Meta-analyses consistently show a two-fold increased risk of subsequent PD in individuals with depressive symptoms or major depressive disorder (MDD), with the highest risk occurring within 1-2 years of diagnosis but persisting for up to 25 years. Late-onset depressive syndrome (after age 50-60) is associated with dopaminergic deficits on dopamine transporter imaging in 24-79% of cases, supporting it as a prodromal symptom, whereas early-onset depression may act through shared genetic vulnerability or chronic inflammatory pathways. Neuroimaging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) reveals that depression correlates with caudate atrophy, frontostriatal white matter disruption, and brainstem monoaminergic dysfunction, but not simply with nigrostriatal denervation. Depression frequently coexists with RBD, autonomic dysfunction, and olfactory impairment, likely reflecting shared brainstem pathology. Genetic forms of PD (GBA1, SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN) show variable depression prevalence, providing mechanistic insights into lysosomal, inflammatory, and proteostatic pathways. Emerging evidence implicates IL-17A, sIL-2R, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation as convergent points linking depression and prodromal α-synucleinopathy, with gut-brain axis dysfunction potentially amplifying this process. Current Movement Disorder Society prodromal PD criteria include depression but have limited sensitivity in general populations. No disease-modifying trials have tested whether treating prodromal depression alters phenoconversion risk. We conclude that proximal, late-onset depressive syndrome is a robust prodromal marker, while distant or early-onset depression, including MDD, identifies a chronically elevated risk population. Future studies should integrate multimodal biomarkers and test therapeutic interventions in prodromal cohorts.

title: [Dual association of peripheral blood eosinophil count with high on-treatment platelet reactivity and long-term cardiac death in patients with coronary artery disease: a large-scale cohort study].
journal: Zhonghua xin xue guan bing za zhi
abstract: Objective: To investigate the association of baseline peripheral blood eosinophil count with high on-treatment platelet reactivity and its clinical prognostic value in patients with coronary artery disease undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and receiving clopidogrel. Methods: This was a single-center prospective cohort study. Consecutive patients with coronary artery disease who underwent PCI at Fuwai Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, between January and December 2013 were enrolled; those receiving dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel were included. Baseline data were collected, and platelet reactivity was assessed using thromboelastography. Patients were followed up for 5 years, with cardiac death as the endpoint. Baseline eosinophil count was analyzed as a continuous variable and was also categorized into quartiles (Q1-Q4). Multivariable logistic regression was used to analyze the association between eosinophil count and high on-treatment platelet reactivity. Multivariable restricted cubic spline models were used to analyze the dose-response relationship. Subgroup analyses and interaction tests were performed according to age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, acute coronary syndrome, body mass index, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression was used to assess the predictive value of eosinophil count for cardiac death. Results: A total of 6 524 patients were included. The mean age was (58.21±10.26) years, and 5 059 (77.54%) were male. Among them, 6 050 patients completed the 5-year follow-up, and 140 cardiac deaths (2.31%) occurred. Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that peripheral blood eosinophil count was negatively associated with the risk of high on-treatment platelet reactivity (OR=0.94, 95%CI: 0.90-0.98, P=0.003). When analyzed as a categorical variable, compared with the lowest quartile group (Q1), the risk of high on-treatment platelet reactivity was lower in patients in the highest quartile group (Q4) (OR=0.77, 95%CI: 0.65-0.91, P=0.003). Multivariable restricted cubic spline analysis showed a linear negative correlation between eosinophil count and the risk of high on-treatment platelet reactivity (P for overall=0.012, P for nonlinearity=0.362). Further subgroup analysis showed that the above association remained consistent across clinical subgroups stratified by age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, acute coronary syndrome, body mass index, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels (all P for interaction>0.05). Multivariable Cox regression analysis showed that peripheral blood eosinophil count was positively associated with the risk of cardiac death (HR=1.14, 95%CI: 1.07-1.21, P<0.001). When analyzed as a categorical variable, compared with the Q1 group, the risk of cardiac death was higher in patients in the Q4 group (HR=2.12, 95%CI: 1.25-3.59, P<0.001). Conclusions: In patients with coronary artery disease undergoing PCI and receiving clopidogrel, baseline peripheral blood eosinophil count showed a dual association with high on-treatment platelet reactivity and long-term cardiac death. A lower count was associated with an increased risk of high on-treatment platelet reactivity, whereas an elevated count was associated with an increased long-term risk of cardiac death.

title: [Mechanistic study of cGAS-STING signaling pathway-mediated blood-brain barrier injury in the prefrontal cortex of 15-month-old mice with postoperative cognitive dysfunction].
abstract: Objective: To investigate the role and mechanism of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway in mediating blood-brain barrier (BBB) injury within the prefrontal cortex of 15-month-old mice with postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD). Methods: Fifteen-month-old male C57BL/6J mice were enrolled and randomly assigned to experimental groups using a random-number table. Experiment 1: twenty-four mice were randomly divided into four groups (n=6): control group (no intervention), sham group, POCD group, and POCD+RU.521 group. On postoperative day 3, cognitive function and spontaneous activity were evaluated by the Morris water maze test and open field test. Prefrontal cortex tissues were subsequently collected for transcriptome sequencing. Experiment 2: twenty-four mice were randomly allocated to eight groups (n=3): sham group, sham+RU.521 group, sham+diABZI group, sham+diABZI+RU.521 group, POCD group, POCD+RU.521 group, POCD+diABZI group, and POCD+diABZI+RU.521 group. On postoperative day 3, prefrontal cortex tissues were harvested for detection of pathway-related protein expression by Western blotting, and assessment of BBB permeability by Evans blue leakage assay. Experiment 3: transcriptome sequencing was performed using prefrontal cortex tissues obtained from experiment 1. Experiment 4: eighteen mice were randomly allocated to three groups (n=6): sham group, POCD group, and POCD+RU.521 group. On postoperative day 3, prefrontal cortex tissues were collected to verify the mRNA expression of target genes by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The POCD model was established by isoflurane anesthesia combined with laparotomy. The cGAS-STING pathway was inhibited or activated by intraperitoneal injection of the cGAS inhibitor RU.521 (5 mg/kg), the STING agonist diABZI (2.5 mg/kg), or diABZI combined with RU.521 at 2 h before surgery, respectively. Results: Compared with the sham group, the POCD group exhibited longer escape latency, lower percentage of time in the target quadrant, and fewer platform crossings in the Morris water maze test, as well as shorter total locomotor distance and less residence time in the central area in the open field test. Compared with the sham group, the relative expression levels of cGAS, STING, p-IRF3 and p-TBK1 in the prefrontal cortex were significantily higher, whereas the relative expression levels of tight junction proteins ZO-1 and Claudin5 were significantily lower, and the Evans blue content in brain tissue was significantily higher in the POCD group (all P<0.05). Intraperitoneal administration of diABZI further aggravated the aforementioned pathway activation, downregulation of tight junction proteins and BBB injury in POCD mice, while intraperitoneal administration of RU.521 reversed these pathological changes and ameliorated cognitive impairment; all these differences were statistically significant (all P<0.05). Compared with the sham group, the sham+diABZI group showed higher expression of cGAS-STING pathway-related proteins and more severe BBB injury, which could be reversed by combined administration with RU.521. Transcriptome sequencing combined with RT-qPCR identified Sdc4, Nnt, Gpt2, Rbp7 and Mertk as relevant target genes. Conclusion: Excessive activation of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway is involved in the pathogenesis of POCD in 15-month-old mice. Inhibition of this pathway can ameliorate postoperative cognitive impairment by alleviating prefrontal cortex blood-brain barrier injury and regulating the expression of relevant target genes.

title: [Identification of risk factors and prevention strategies for perioperative stroke].
abstract: Perioperative stroke refers to embolic, thrombotic, or hemorrhagic cerebrovascular disease occurring during surgery or within 30 days postoperatively, which can lead to disability or death in patients. This review systematically describes the pathogenesis, risk factor identification, and prevention and treatment strategies for perioperative stroke. The pathogenesis of perioperative ischemic stroke involves multiple pathological processes including thromboembolism, hemodynamic disturbances, inflammatory responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption. Risk factors include patient-related factors, surgical factors, and anesthesia management factors. Prevention strategies emphasize preoperative precise identification of high-risk patients using risk assessment tools and predictive models, optimizing control of underlying diseases; intraoperative maintenance of hemodynamic stability, implementation of cerebral oxygen saturation monitoring, and timely detection of cerebral ischemia; postoperative establishment of neurological function monitoring systems, adoption of standardized stroke screening tools to achieve early identification and timely intervention. Establishing multidisciplinary collaboration mechanisms, implementing effective perioperative management, and exploring novel neuroprotective targets and intervention strategies are key to reducing perioperative stroke incidence and improving patient outcomes.

title: [Strategies for perioperative pain management and the prevention and management of postoperative delirium in frail older patients].
abstract: Postoperative pain and postoperative delirium (POD) may share some pathophysiological mechanisms in frail older patients. Persistent nociceptive input, accumulation of analgesic drugs, hemodynamic fluctuations, and respiratory depression may increase the risk of acute brain dysfunction. Potential mechanisms include blood-brain barrier disruption and neuroinflammation, disturbances in cerebral perfusion and oxygen metabolism, and disruption of sleep and arousal networks. A systematic review suggests a dose-response relationship between postoperative pain intensity and POD, although the certainty of the evidence is low and causality remains unproven. This article proposes a "dual-exposure, three-pathway, closed-loop management" framework for perioperative analgesia and the prevention and management of postoperative delirium in frail older patients. Preoperative assessment should include frailty, cognitive status, and pain-related risk. Intraoperatively, precision multimodal analgesia should be tailored to incisional, visceral, and inflammatory pain, with the regimen adjusted using data from nociception, electroencephalographic, cerebral oxygenation, and hemodynamic monitoring. Postoperatively, pain should be assessed repeatedly over time, together with concurrent screening for POD and identification of reversible precipitating factors. The goal of analgesia in frail older patients should not be defined simply as "zero pain" or complete avoidance of opioids. Instead, adequate analgesia should be provided while minimizing treatment-related adverse effects that may impair brain function.

title: The Roles and Uses of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroimmunologic Diseases.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Neuroimmunology is a field of neurology focused on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases where the immune system causes inflammation or injury to the nervous system. This includes diseases such as multiple sclerosis, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune ataxia, stiff person syndrome spectrum disorder, and neuro-rheumatologic diseases such as neuropsychiatric lupus. Over the past couple decades, there have been significant advancements in the diagnostic methods for several neuroimmunologic diseases. Despite these achievements, major needs remain for additional methods to facilitate earlier diagnosis, monitor disease activity and treatment, and elucidate disease mechanisms to aid in the development of novel or tailored treatment strategies. Currently, there is often a trade-off between the invasiveness of neurodiagnostic testing and the level of detail that can be obtained from the test without causing an iatrogenic injury. Here, we discuss the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), especially CNS-derived EVs obtained from peripheral blood, as a promising avenue for advancing research and clinical care in neuroimmunology. This article provides a review of the key clinical features and approaches to care for the most common neuroimmunologic diseases. We identify gaps that remain in our current understanding of these conditions. We then highlight how ongoing research in the EV field may address these existing gaps. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be overcome before EV analysis can be more widely adopted in both research and clinical care in this field.
keywords: Autoimmune Diseases of the Nervous System

title: Beyond Dissemination: From Critical Science Literacy to Citizen Neuroscience.
abstract: Neuroscience increasingly informs education, mental health, and public policy, yet its real-world impact remains limited, with misunderstandings and neuromyths persisting. We argue that the societal impact of neuroscience communication depends less on the volume of information disseminated than on whether it cultivates critical science literacy, namely, the ability to evaluate how neuroscientific knowledge is generated, modeled, and constrained and to understand the inferential steps linking data to conclusions and their limits of generalization. In the context of neuroscience, we refer to this as critical neuroscience literacy to emphasize the domain-specific challenges of interpreting brain-based evidence. The primary barrier is not insufficient dissemination alone, but systematic misinterpretation of neuroscientific inference once findings leave the laboratory. We advance three claims: first, that public misunderstandings often reflect limited insight into scientific reasoning and practice rather than simple information deficits about scientific results; second, that citizen science and dialogical engagement function as mechanisms for practicing such reasoning rather than as outreach add-ons; and third, that neuroscientists share responsibility for shaping the interpretive conditions under which findings are translated, particularly in education, health, and policy. Importantly, this self-referentiality is not merely descriptive. Interpretations are associated with beliefs, expectations, and environments that may themselves be linked to neural and behavioral change. We outline implications for training, incentives, and professional norms within the neuroscience community.

title: Cohort profile: the Swedish Evaluation Through Follow-up Study of Learning Later in Life (UGU-LIFE).
Best Practices for Anesthetic Management and Analgesia for the Patient Undergoing Amputation.
abstract: This review article summarizes best practices for the anesthetic management and analgesia of patients undergoing limb amputation, populations in which acute stump pain and chronic phantom limb pain are highly prevalent. Organized across the perioperative continuum, it examines preoperative pain optimization and preemptive analgesia, intraoperative anesthetic technique selection and pharmacologic adjuncts such as ketamine and alpha-2 agonists, and postoperative regional and multimodal systemic analgesia. The authors also address long-term phantom limb pain through neuroplasticity-based retraining. They conclude that optimal care is multimodal, perioperative, and multidisciplinary, targeting both nociceptive and neuropathic mechanisms to improve short-term and long-term outcomes.

title: Ketamine in Modern Medicine: Current Evidence in Acute Pain, Opioid Use Disorder, and Depression.
abstract: Ketamine has continued to be a valuable adjunct in perioperative care, supported by recent meta-analyses demonstrating opioid-sparing effects and improved analgesia, particularly in opioid-tolerant patients and painful surgeries. Its use should be targeted to patients most likely to benefit from its unique properties. Beyond acute pain, ketamine shows promise in patients with opioid use disorder by mitigating tolerance and withdrawal through N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor modulation and downstream neuroadaptive effects. Additionally, its established antidepressant properties position ketamine as a potentially advantageous agent for patients with coexisting pain and mood disorders, a population frequently encountered in perioperative practice.

title: Optimizing Clozapine Use Through Therapeutic Drug Monitoring-Integrating Clinical and Laboratory Science Perspectives.
abstract: Clozapine, a second-generation antipsychotic, remains the most effective pharmacologic option for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, though it remains underutilized due to multiple factors, including patient concerns about adverse effects and limited prescriber familiarity with its optimal use. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is highly recommended for clozapine and can support individualized dosing, enhance safety, and improve clinical decision making by providing an objective measure of drug exposure. This article reviews the clinical application of clozapine TDM alongside laboratory methodologies, including immunoassays and mass spectrometry, highlighting how integration of clinical and laboratory perspectives can improve clozapine treatment.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, Premenstrual Syndrome, and Premenstrual Exacerbation.
journal: Endocrinology and metabolism clinics of North America
abstract: Premenstrual symptoms occur in the late luteal phase as a result of differential sensitivity to normal hormonal fluctuations. These symptoms can include mood symptoms such as mood lability, anxiety, sadness or irritability as well as physical symptoms such as lethargy, bloating and breast tenderness. Symptoms can significantly impact quality of life, particularly in patients with the more severe form of premenstrual symptoms, PMDD. Importantly, symptoms should improve or resolve in the follicular phase. Evidence-based treatment options include SSRIs or hormonal suppression of ovulation with COCs or GnRH agonists.

title: Papilloedema, transverse venous sinus stenosis and acquired Chiari I malformation associated with vitamin A deficiency in a child.
Comparative neuropathological evaluation of pT217 immunoreactivity in human and transgenic mouse tauopathies.
journal: Journal of neuropathology and experimental neurology
abstract: Tau phosphorylation at threonine 217 (pT217) has been increasingly recognized as a biomarker for Alzheimer disease (AD), but its neuropathological distribution and the performance of available antibodies remain to be fully characterized. In this study, we performed a comparative evaluation of a recombinant rabbit monoclonal anti-pT217 antibody (mAb) using immunohistochemical and biochemical analyzes in human and transgenic mouse tauopathies and compared results to those of a commercially available anti-pT217 antibody and the AT8 antibody. In rTg4510 mice, the anti-pT217 mAb detected pathological tau aggregates with high sensitivity, including hyperphosphorylated tau species identified by biochemical fraction. In human postmortem brain tissues (AD, Pick disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration), quantitative image analysis demonstrated labeling of a broad range of tau lesions, including neurofibrillary tangles, neuropil threads, tufted astrocytes, astrocytic plaques, and Pick bodies. The overall detectability was comparable to that of AT8 and similar to or modestly > that of a representative commercial anti-pT217 antibody. These findings indicate that pT217 is widely present across tauopathies and suggest that the recombinant anti-pT217 mAb provides a sensitive and reproducible tool for neuropathological assessment. Together, these results provide a framework for evaluating anti-pT217 antibodies in neuropathological studies.
